entry.summary: Most applications eventually face login problems that have little to do with their core purpose. Users forget passwords, reuse credentials, and struggle with account recovery. Meanwhile, developers must consider credential security, brute-force protection, and session management. This is the reason why I started looking into passwordless authentication and how passkeys can potentially alter the login experience. The idea is simple: users should be able to prove their identity without typing a conventional password every time they sign in. Passkeys use public-key cryptography through standards such as WebAuthn. entry.summary: Somewhere in the first hour of reading about AI agents, you meet a diagram. A box labelled Thought, an arrow to Action, an arrow to Observation, and an arrow curling back to the start. The captions say the agent reasons, plans and decides. It makes building one sound like work for a research lab. Then someone asks a plain question: when the agent "thinks", what does the model actually receive? The honest answer is a list of messages, written as JSON, sent in an ordinary web request. The reply is more JSON. Nothing in between remembers anything. That gap, between the vocabulary and the mechanism, is what this primer closes: six ideas, explained from zero, each with something you can see for yourself. entry.title: AI Chatbot Refund Policy: Stop Disputes Before They Start
entry.summary: An agent that promises a refund it cannot authorize turns a support tool into a liability. Here are the six cases it must always escalate and the rule wording it can actually follow. At 9:12 p.m. a customer typed one line into a website chat: can I get a refund? The agent answered two seconds later: "Of course — I've approved a full refund and it will be back on your card within 3–5 days." The agent had no refund authority and no way to issue one. The business found out three days later, when the customer pasted that message back and asked where their money was. One sentence, sent at night, with nobody watching. entry.title: We open-sourced the tool that failed its own kill rule
entry.summary: Before we ran the experiment, we wrote down the rule that would kill it. The product under test was a pipeline that builds skill files for AI agents: those structured instruction documents, SKILL.md and friends, that tell an agent when to trigger, what to do, and what never to do.
